claims.text: Conventional EAM references do not represent the diverse atomic configurations present in ab initio liquids.
An on-the-fly machine-learning correction to an EAM potential will improve reference–target phase-space overlap for high-entropy-alloy liquids.
The ML-augmented EAM reference will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to conventional TOR-TILD EAM references.
The proposed reference potential is trained and updated using representative high-temperature ab initio liquid configurations.
The intervention is applicable to refractory multicomponent alloys, including tungsten-based alloys containing elements such as Re and Ir.
The applicable temperature range is approximately 80% to 90% of the alloy melting temperature.
Liquid-like atomic configurations become significant at approximately 80% to 90% of the melting temperature.
The machine-learning model can identify and correct EAM errors in predicted energies and forces for configurations outside the usual EAM parameter space.
Correcting those errors bridges the gap between EAM configurational sampling and the ab initio energy landscape.
Iterative training on ab initio molecular-dynamics data for the liquid state improves force-field accuracy.
Improved force-field accuracy increases reference–target phase-space overlap.
Increased phase-space overlap reduces the discrepancy between the thermodynamic-integration path and true liquid behavior.
Reducing thermodynamic-integration path discrepancy produces a more faithful free-energy surface.
The ML-augmented reference will reduce integration-path error by at least 30% relative to standard TOR-TILD EAM references.
The ML-augmented reference will agree more closely with ab initio free-energy benchmarks than a conventional EAM reference.
The intervention will be most effective for multicomponent alloys with moderately complex electronic interactions.
Strong electronic effects or temperatures substantially below the liquid regime may make the ML correction insufficient.
The approach may not generalize when important phase-space phenomena are absent from the training data.
Failure to reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by at least 30% would falsify the hypothesis.
